walkthrough:
Read the fate of each cell from the diagram**
U4 ends with release of cell-signalling molecules to coordinate other cells. V4 ends by attaching directly to an infected cell to destroy it. Those two jobs define the two main types of active T cell.

Match job to name**
The signalling, coordinating cell is the helper. The cell that contacts and kills infected cells is the killer, also called cytotoxic. So U4 is helper and V4 is killer.
Final answer: U4 is T-helper lymphocyte / cell; V4 is T-killer / T-cytotoxic lymphocyte / cell.

Recall that one type of T cell acts as a coordinator by secreting soluble messengers, while the other acts as an effector that contacts its target.
For the coordinator, think which other immune cells need stimulating - B-lymphocytes to make antibody and phagocytes to be more active.
For the attacker, think what toxic chemicals are released onto infected cells and how they cause pores and protein breakdown leading to death.
walkthrough:
Role of U4 as coordinator**
U4 does not kill itself. It releases cell-signalling molecules called cytokines, for example interleukins. Think of these as chemical instructions that switch on other immune cells.

Who U4 stimulates**
Those cytokines stimulate B-lymphocytes to divide by mitosis and develop into plasma cells for antibody production, which is clonal expansion and the humoral response. They also stimulate macrophages to become highly active phagocytes.

Role of V4 as direct killer**
V4 binds to an infected body cell and releases toxic chemicals directly onto it to kill the infected cell before virus can replicate further. This is cell-mediated killing, leading to lysis or apoptosis.

Name chemicals and their action**
Key examples are perforin, which makes pores in the cell surface membrane of the infected cell, and granzymes / proteases, which enter through the pores and break down proteins to trigger death. Hydrogen peroxide that oxidises cell components is another valid example.

Final answer: U4 / helper secretes cytokines / interleukins to stimulate B-lymphocytes to divide / develop into plasma cells and to stimulate macrophages to carry out phagocytosis. V4 / killer secretes chemicals such as perforin and granzymes / proteases to kill infected cells, e.g. perforin makes pores in the cell surface membrane and granzymes break down proteins / induce apoptosis.

hints: Think about what eradication means - zero cases everywhere, so coverage must be global and include hard-to-reach groups, not just cities.
Think about barriers to uptake - cost, supply, trained staff and public trust - and what health authorities can do to remove them.
Think about immunity at population level - why a very high proportion must be immune at the same time and why early vaccination plus boosters matters.
Think about finding the last cases - records, surveillance, contact tracing and rapid ring vaccination around any new case.
walkthrough:
Make vaccine accessible to everyone**
Eradication needs no pockets of susceptible people left. Authorities must provide enough vaccine, free of charge, to urban and rural populations worldwide, with funding, trained staff and cold chain to keep vaccine effective.

Achieve herd immunity**
Vaccinate a very high proportion of the population, starting with children as early as possible, and give boosters where needed. When most people are immune, transmission chains break and the pathogen cannot find new hosts, which protects even the few who cannot be vaccinated.

Track who is protected and find disease fast**
Keep accurate records to identify anyone missed. Carry out surveillance and contact tracing to look for any cases, and monitor the success of the programme.

Respond and persuade**
Vaccinate immediately around any new case, known as ring immunity, and quarantine cases if needed. Provide education about how the disease spreads, its severe effects like paralysis, and the safety and benefits of vaccination to counter misinformation.

Final answer: Any four: make vaccine free and available globally to whole population; vaccinate a high proportion to achieve herd immunity; vaccinate children early and provide boosters / use effective live attenuated vaccine; keep accurate records to find unvaccinated; surveillance / contact tracing with immediate / ring vaccination around cases; educate about disease effects and vaccine benefits; ensure sufficient supply, funding, trained personnel and cold chain.
